title: Muslim Separatism: Causes and Consequences
byline: by Sita Ram Goel · Voice of India · 1987, enlarged 1995
lede: Most studies of Partition, Goel says, recite the same account: British divide-and-rule, Muslim fears of “Hindu domination” after 1885, and the League as a reaction to Hindu revivalism. He welcomes H.V. Seshadri's The Tragic Story of Partition as “a breath of fresh breeze” and builds on it. His argument is that Partition came from two behaviour patterns that both continued after 1947. One is Muslim separatism, which he traces to Islam itself rather than to the British. The other is a national leadership that answered every demand with a concession.

note: Goel's reading of Partition is a minority one. Most historians give more weight to British policy, the politics of the Congress and the League, and the events of 1946–47. This page summarises his argument, attributed to him.
